title: India Pulls Off Largest-Ever Stake Sale With Rs 31,552 Crore LIC OFS
excerpt: The government raised more than double its original target by selling a 6.5% stake in LIC through a tightly guarded Offer for Sale, pushing public shareholding to 10% ahead of the regulatory deadline.
body:
• The government raised Rs 31,552 crore by selling a 6.5% stake in LIC — India's largest-ever public offering by issue size
  • LIC's public shareholding rose to 10%, meeting SEBI's minimum threshold well ahead of the May 2027 deadline
  • The OFS was oversubscribed on both days, with institutional demand at 3.32 times the base offer and shares allotted at Rs 383.69 against a floor of Rs 382
  • The government kept the sale date secret even from its own advising bankers until hours before launch

The Indian government completed its largest-ever secondary share sale through a stock exchange this month, raising Rs 31,552 crore by divesting a 6.5% stake in Life Insurance Corporation of India. The Offer for Sale, executed on August 4-5, more than doubled the government's original target and became the biggest public offering in Indian capital markets history by issue size.

A Sale Kept Secret Until the Last Hour

The scale of the transaction was matched by the secrecy surrounding its execution. According to a Bloomberg report, officials at the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) withheld the launch date from virtually everyone — including the four banks advising on the deal — to prevent traders from taking short positions that could depress LIC's stock price ahead of the sale.

"With this the public ownership of LIC has increased to 10 per cent and it has achieved this critical milestone ahead of schedule."

— DIPAM, via post on X

The OFS was managed by IIFL Capital Services, BNP Paribas Securities India, Goldman Sachs India, and Motilal Oswal Investment Advisors. One banker was summoned to DIPAM's office in New Delhi hours before the sale opened without being told why. Only on arrival was the banker informed that the LIC stake sale would begin that evening, and asked to immediately prepare the exchange filing. The remaining advisers were brought in only after markets closed for the day.

None of the four advisers charged a fee for the deal. During the request-for-proposal process, one bank had agreed to work for free, which eventually led all four to forgo their fees — a pattern common in government-linked transactions where prestige and long-term relationships take precedence.

Strong Demand Across Both Days

The government initially offered a base 2.5% stake with a greenshoe option to sell an additional 4%. The base portion was subscribed 3.32 times by institutional investors on August 4, prompting the government to exercise the full greenshoe option. Retail investors bid on August 5, with the retail portion subscribed 69%.

Overall, the offering was subscribed 1.2 times. Against the 82.23 crore shares on offer (including the greenshoe), total demand stood at 111.3 crore shares. The final allotment price came in at Rs 383.69 per share, slightly above the floor price of Rs 382.

DIPAM Secretary Arunish Chawla noted on X that the strong response reflected investor confidence in both LIC and the government's broader disinvestment programme.

Meeting Regulatory Norms Ahead of Schedule

Before the OFS, the government held 96.5% of LIC, leaving just 3.5% with public shareholders. The sale reduced the government's stake to 90%, raising LIC's public shareholding to 10% and satisfying SEBI's minimum public shareholding requirement well ahead of the May 2027 regulatory deadline.

LIC, India's largest life insurer, was listed on the stock exchanges in May 2022 after a scaled-down IPO. The latest OFS represents the most significant step in expanding the company's public float since that listing.

Market Impact and Timing

LIC shares initially dropped nearly 8% on August 4 when the OFS was announced, hitting an intraday low of Rs 390.70 on the BSE. The floor price of Rs 382 represented an approximately 11% discount to LIC's previous closing price, which weighed on sentiment.

However, by the time the offering closed and shares were allotted, the stock stabilized. LIC closed at Rs 393 on the NSE following the completion of the sale, recovering modestly. The government's decision to launch before LIC's quarterly earnings — which most participants had expected to be the trigger — was a calculated move to maintain uncertainty around timing and keep the stock price stable through the execution window.

Market analysts view the successful OFS as a boost to the government's FY27 disinvestment programme, while the deeper public float is expected to attract greater institutional participation and improve liquidity in LIC shares going forward.
nri_angle: LIC remains one of the most widely held financial products among the Indian diaspora, and the increased public float could improve liquidity for NRI investors holding or looking to trade LIC shares.
author: Diaspora Desk
